items.source: McKinsey Global Institute — Chart of the Week
items.title: Global household wealth hit $570 trillion in 2025 — and 80% of the growth was fake
items.idea: Total global wealth across all sectors hit $600T in 2025 (households own 95% of it). Household wealth alone hit a record $570T, up $40T from 2024. Only 20% of that gain came from real capital formation — the rest is asset revaluation, with equity values driving growth in the US and Canada. US holds 30% of global household wealth, eurozone 14%, China 13%.
items.angle: This is the AI-capex-into-equity-wealth-into-consumption loop quantified at the global level — roughly $32T of the $40T wealth gain last year was paper gains, not new production.
items.tweetA: $40T added to global household wealth in 2025. $32T of it — 80% — was asset repricing, not real capital formation. This is what 'wealth effect' consumption is actually funded by right now.
items.tweetB: The US holds 30% of $570T in global household wealth with about 4% of world population. That concentration is the AI-capex story from a different angle — the equity gains are landing overwhelmingly on one country's household balance sheets.

charts.desc: Featured chart on global assets/liabilities/wealth by sector and region — the $40T YoY breakdown by capital formation vs revaluation is the money shot.

items.title: Goldman's hedge fund crowding monitor: AI longs stay crowded, shorts pile in on top
items.idea: Goldman PB's monthly hedge fund crowding monitor shows a near mirror-image flip from a month ago — shorts building aggressively in Broad AI and Data Centers, while Software just had a rare bullish flip. Funds aren't exiting AI longs; they're layering shorts and hedges on top of already-crowded exposure.
items.angle: When the same desk shows crowded longs and fresh shorts building in the same names, the next big move — either direction — gets amplified as both sides unwind.
items.tweetA: Same hedge funds, same AI longs, now adding shorts on top. That's not de-risking, that's hedging a position they won't sell. When crowded longs meet crowded new shorts in the same basket, the next move gets violent.
items.tweetB: Software just had a 'rare bullish flip' in positioning while Data Centers get shorted. The market is quietly rotating within AI — picking the picks-and-shovels layer over the infrastructure layer. Nobody's calling that split loudly yet.

items.source: Peter Frankopan
items.title: New genomic research rewrites how smallpox actually killed the Americas
items.idea: A new Science paper (Romero González et al.) maps genomic divergence in smallpox strains that proved lethal in the Americas after 1492. Smallpox killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone before eradication in 1980; in the Americas it killed at least 3–4 million (possibly far more) — first documented Caribbean 1518, Mexico 1520, the Andes 1525 — a demographic collapse Frankopan argues was worse than the Black Death.
items.angle: Pattern-recognition angle: the mechanism (immunologically naive population + novel pathogen strain divergence, not just introduction) is the same framework epidemiologists use for pandemic risk modeling today.
items.tweetA: New genomic data says it wasn't just 'Europeans brought smallpox' — specific strain divergence made it more lethal once it hit the Americas. The collapse (3–4M+ dead, arguably worse than the Black Death) was a strain-specific event, not an inevitability of contact alone.
items.tweetB: 1518 Caribbean, 1520 Mexico, 1525 Andes — a virus crossed the Atlantic and reshaped two continents in seven years. Worth remembering next time someone calls genomic surveillance for emerging pathogens overkill.

charts.desc: No chart in this email preview — likely a genomic phylogenetic tree in the underlying Science paper.

items.title: The US economy's growth machinery is now an AI trade, not a bystander to one
items.idea: Hyperscaler capex is now large enough to independently move US fixed investment and GDP growth. The framing isn't whether NVDA is expensive — it's that capex, equity wealth, and consumption have become increasingly connected to the same underlying trade, echoing the late-1990s telecom buildout where capital spending ran far ahead of realized returns.
items.angle: Combine with the McKinsey wealth chart — the AI capex cycle is now double-counted into GDP: once through investment, again through the equity-wealth-effect on consumption. That's leverage on leverage if the trade turns.
items.tweetA: If hyperscaler capex alone can move US GDP prints, a capex pause from two or three companies is now a macro event, not a sector event. Nobody's stress-testing the Fed's growth forecast for that.
items.tweetB: The AI trade shows up in GDP twice: once when Microsoft builds the datacenter, again when the resulting equity gains get spent by households holding NVDA/MSFT stock. Two transmission channels, one underlying asset — the 1999 telecom setup with an extra leg.

items.source: Wajahat Mughal (Starcap)
items.title: Launch cost fell 90%+ in two decades and the curve hasn't flattened
items.idea: Falcon 9 Block 5 launch cost sits near $1,500/kg today, down from ~$3,700/kg (2015 Falcon 9 v1.1) and five-to-six-figure per-kg costs before that. Starship is currently estimated at $900/kg with credible projections under $200/kg later this decade at ~10 flights/vehicle. SpaceX flew 165 orbital missions in 2025 — roughly one every two days, carrying 80%+ of all mass humanity put into orbit that year — versus the entire 30-year Space Shuttle program's 135 flights total.
items.angle: The 'cost curve' argument for space as an investable infrastructure layer has the same shape as the cloud-compute cost curve that preceded the SaaS boom — except almost nobody outside space-specialist funds is pricing it in yet.
items.tweetA: SpaceX put more mass into orbit in 2025 than the entire 30-year Space Shuttle program combined — in a single year. Nobody's GDP model or capex forecast has 'orbit becomes a cheap, boring commodity' as a line item yet.
items.tweetB: $1,500/kg today, sub-$200/kg projected by end of decade. That's not a rocket story anymore, that's a cost-curve story — the same shape as compute costs before the cloud buildout. The rocket was never the investable asset; what gets built on top of cheap orbit is.

charts.desc: No embedded chart — long-form essay; cost-curve data is in the text (worth charting: launch $/kg 2005-2026).

items.source: Wajahat Mughal (Starcap)
items.title: SpaceX filed to put 1 million compute satellites in orbit — because deep space is a free, infinite heat sink
items.idea: SpaceX has filed to deploy up to one million compute satellites targeting 100 gigawatts of capacity per year by 2030, with prototypes flying 2027. The pitch: orbital datacenters solve power (continuous sun, no grid queue), cooling (radiate into a heat sink 3 degrees above absolute zero, zero water), land, and permitting simultaneously. Google is flying prototype TPUs (Project Suncatcher); Starcloud has already run an Nvidia H100 in orbit and trained the first LLM in space.
items.angle: Every one of the four bottlenecks currently strangling US datacenter buildout — grid interconnect queues, water use, land/zoning fights, permitting — disappears in orbit. If even 10% of this materializes, it directly relieves the exact constraints everyone worries will cap AI capex growth.
items.tweetA: The binding constraint on AI right now isn't chips, it's grid interconnect queues measured in years and water tables measured in millions of gallons. SpaceX's answer: skip the grid, skip the water, put the datacenter where the sun never sets. 1 million satellites filed.
items.tweetB: Starcloud already trained an LLM on a GPU in orbit. Everyone arguing about whether datacenters get banned on Earth for water/power use is arguing about a constraint that may simply route around itself within 5 years.

charts.desc: No chart embedded — worth pulling SpaceX's filing numbers (satellites, GW target, timeline) into a visual.

items.source: Wajahat Mughal (Starcap)
items.title: A square meter of solar panel in orbit produces 5-6x more power than on Earth
items.idea: Above the atmosphere, sunlight delivers 1,361 W/m² (the solar constant); after atmospheric loss, weather, and night, a strong terrestrial solar farm averages 200-250 W/m². Combine intensity with 24/7 duration in the right orbit and you get 5-6x more annual energy per panel. The buyer ladder starts with satellites themselves (paying thousands of $/watt), then off-grid military/remote/disaster customers, then terrestrial mirror extension, with grid-scale beaming last. First commercial power-beaming missions fly in 2026.
items.angle: This reframes space solar from the 1960s sci-fi 'beam gigawatts to the grid' framing into a normal land-and-expand strategy — start with the highest-willingness-to-pay customer and work down the value chain.
items.tweetA: Space solar died as an idea in the 1960s because everyone tried to solve 'beam gigawatts to the grid' first. The sequencing being built now: sell power to satellites first (they already pay thousands of $/watt), then off-grid military, then grid-scale. First missions fly in 2026.
items.tweetB: 5-6x more energy per panel in orbit than on Earth, and the first paying customer is already up there: other satellites. This is a normal enterprise land-and-expand motion wearing a space-opera costume.

charts.desc: No chart embedded — the buyer-ladder concept (satellites > off-grid > mirrors > grid) is a natural chart if you open the article.

items.source: Wajahat Mughal (Starcap)
items.title: Merck crystallized Keytruda in orbit — and got a uniform result gravity can't produce on Earth
items.idea: In microgravity, liquids don't convection-mix, so crystals form slowly and evenly from every direction. When Merck crystallized the antibody in Keytruda (the world's best-selling cancer drug) aboard the ISS, it produced a uniform suspension clustered at 39 micrometers — precise enough to potentially convert an hours-long hospital IV infusion into an at-home injection. United Therapeutics is now putting its own capital into microgravity formulation work with Varda, whose reentry capsules crystallize drugs in orbit and fly them home; first commercial pharma flight targeted 2027.
items.angle: A patent-life-extension and delivery-mechanism play as much as a manufacturing one — a 'better crystal' of an existing biologic is a new formulation, which means new IP on drugs already generating billions in revenue.
items.tweetA: Merck put its best-selling cancer drug in zero gravity and got a more uniform crystal than any factory on Earth can produce — precise enough to potentially turn an IV infusion into a shot you give yourself at home. That's a patent-extension story wearing a space story's clothes.
items.tweetB: United Therapeutics is now funding microgravity drug manufacturing with its own balance sheet, not a grant. When a pharma company puts cash behind orbital R&D instead of a press release, that's the signal worth tracking, not the ISS photo.

charts.desc: No chart embedded — worth visualizing the 39-micrometer uniform crystal result vs Earth-gravity crystal distribution.

items.source: Wajahat Mughal (Starcap)
items.title: The space stack is quietly raising nine-figure rounds across every layer
items.idea: Capital is stacking across the full orbital value chain: Varda (microgravity pharma) $300M+, Starcloud (orbital compute) $200M+, Axiom Space (infrastructure) closed $525M in 2026, Vast (commercial station) raised a first external round of $500M on top of founder Jed McCaleb's own $1B, Relativity Space (heavy-lift) $1.3B raised against $3B of contracts waiting on capacity, K2 Space $500M Series D, Isar Aerospace (European sovereign launch) €870M — the most of any European launch startup.
items.angle: Capital is diversifying across the stack (launch, compute, pharma, power, station, logistics) rather than concentrating in one 'space bet' — that pattern is what infrastructure buildouts look like right before the sector goes mainstream.
items.tweetA: Nine-figure rounds across launch, orbital compute, microgravity pharma, station infrastructure, and power — all in the same 12 months. That's not one company getting hyped, that's an entire stack getting built simultaneously. That pattern preceded cloud, it preceded EVs.
items.tweetB: $1.3B into Relativity for heavy lift, against $3B of contracts already waiting on capacity they don't have yet. Demand is ahead of supply in this sector right now — that's the setup you want to be early to, not late to.

items.title: Senate passed a 90-6 funding patch that quietly blocks Trump's grant-control overhaul
items.idea: The Senate passed a continuing resolution 90-6, funding agencies through Dec 11 at current levels, then left for a 5-week recess — shifting the shutdown-avoidance burden entirely to the House before the Sept 30 deadline. Buried in the bill: language that would temporarily block the administration's grant-control overhaul, turning routine appropriations text into a check on OMB/political-appointee control over scientific funding. White House priorities (voting legislation, added spending) were left out because they lacked the 60 votes to survive.
items.angle: A 90-6 vote is Congress explicitly avoiding the fight, not resolving it — it just moved the shutdown risk (and the executive-power fight over grants) to December, past the point most people are watching.
items.tweetA: 90-6 isn't consensus, it's avoidance. The Senate just kicked the shutdown fight to Dec 11 and left town for 5 weeks. The House is now the sole chokepoint on a funding bill it didn't write and can't easily amend without reopening every fight the Senate stripped out.
items.tweetB: Buried in a routine funding patch: language blocking the White House's grant-control overhaul. Congress just used appropriations text to check executive power over science funding without a single headline calling it that.

items.title: Goldman: the July jobs miss didn't kill the Fed hike case — it moved the burden to inflation

items.tweetB: Three different currencies, three different rate calls from the same desk: US steepeners, EUR front-end flattening vs US, pay JPY 5y5y vs EUR. That's a coordinated global rates view, not three separate country calls — the common thread is US real-yield leadership.

items.source: The Bond Beat (weekly roundup)
items.title: July NFP: -23K vs +80K expected, biggest miss on the board, and Wall Street partied anyway
items.idea: Payrolls fell 23K in July against an +80K consensus (every economist on the Street missed low), with May/June revised down another 103K combined — the largest two-month revision since July 2025's -258K. Wages rose just 0.1% m/m (3.2% y/y, below the 3.5% estimate). Unemployment still fell to 4.1% purely because labor force participation dropped to 61.4% — the lowest since the 1970s excluding the pandemic. September hike odds fell from ~55% to ~44%. S&P 500 posted its best week since April on the print.
items.angle: A falling unemployment rate driven by shrinking labor supply, not rising demand, is a different economy than the one the rally is pricing — the 'bad news is good news' trade just survived a report that missed every economist's forecast, which says more about positioning than about the data.
items.tweetA: Every economist on Bloomberg forecast a positive NFP print. It came in at -23K. The S&P had its best week since April. At some point 'bad news is good news' stops being a thesis and starts being a hedge everyone's afraid to be caught without.
items.tweetB: Unemployment fell to 4.1% in July for the worst possible reason: the labor force shrank to its lowest participation rate since the 1970s. That's not 'full employment,' that's people leaving the workforce. The rate and the story it's telling have diverged.

charts.desc: NFP miss vs consensus, revisions, and 2-year full-time-jobs low charts referenced (via ZH) — worth pulling.

items.source: The Bond Beat (via BAML Global Rates Weekly)
items.title: Foreign central banks now own just 12% of Treasuries, down from 31% in 2016
items.idea: BAML notes that during both the 2024 and April/May 2026 JPY intervention episodes, front-end swap spreads actually richened despite foreign official Treasury sales — the opposite of the historical pattern. Their explanation: foreign officials now hold just 12% of Treasuries outstanding (down from 31% in 2016) and have been net sellers for years. The marginal UST buyer today is foreign private investors and domestic funds, not reserve managers — meaning Treasury valuations are now far more sensitive to bank/fund demand than official-sector flows.
items.angle: This is a structural plumbing shift that changes how every future BoJ/PBOC intervention should be read — the 'someone's selling Treasuries to defend their currency, that's bearish for USTs' playbook from 2015-2022 may no longer apply.
items.tweetA: Foreign central banks holding Treasuries has gone from 31% to 12% since 2016. Every 'the BoJ/PBOC intervention will dump Treasuries' take from the 2010s is now running on a market structure that doesn't exist anymore.
items.tweetB: Swap spreads richened during the last two JPY intervention episodes instead of cheapening — the exact opposite of the textbook reaction. When data stops matching the model, the model is describing a market that already moved on. Watch bank and fund demand now, not central bank flows.

charts.desc: BAML Exhibit 7 referenced — foreign official Treasury holding share over time. Worth pulling.

items.source: The Bond Beat (via Morgan Stanley US Rates Strategy)
items.title: Morgan Stanley's technical call: US 10-year yields are in a 5th wave targeting 5.50-5.75%
items.idea: MS notes July's monthly close on US10Y above 4.62% resolved a 2.5-year triangle consolidation to the upside — they read it as the fifth Elliott wave higher from the 2020 low, with potential for yields to reach 5.50-5.75% over time, provided the May 2026 low of 4.45% holds as support. Longer-term, a 38.2% retracement of the entire 1981-2020 secular yield decline would eventually put 10-year yields near 6.25%.
items.angle: A pure technical call sitting apart from every fundamental steepener/flattener thesis in the same roundup — if MS's chartists are right, the 'Fed on hold, disinflation continues' macro consensus and the technical picture point in opposite directions on where 10s ultimately land.
items.tweetA: Every fundamental desk in this roundup is debating whether the Fed hikes 25bp in September. Morgan Stanley's chartists are debating whether the 10-year eventually retraces to 6.25%. Two entirely different magnitudes of 'higher for longer' being priced by the same bank simultaneously.
items.tweetB: A 2.5-year triangle just resolved upward on the 10-year's monthly chart. Technicians don't care why — they care that 4.62% held as a monthly close. If that's right, next week's CPI print is noise against the real move.

items.title: Atlanta Fed's first Q3 GDP estimate: 5.9% — two days after a negative jobs print
items.idea: Atlanta Fed GDPNow's opening bid for Q3 GDP is 5.9%, per the roundup, despite the July payroll report showing a headline job loss. Early GDPNow reads are historically noisy and converge as more data arrives within the quarter, but the framing stands in stark contrast to the 'bad news is good news' jobs narrative dominating the same week.
items.angle: The market narrative (soft jobs = dovish Fed = bullish stocks) and the growth data (5.9% GDPNow) are telling contradictory stories simultaneously — if GDPNow holds anywhere close to that level, the 'Fed needs to cut/hold because growth is weakening' case gets much harder to make by September.

items.tweetB: GDPNow's first read is always the least reliable one, but 5.9% next to a headline job loss is a big enough gap that it's worth watching whether the two series converge toward the growth number or the jobs number as August data lands.

items.source: The Bond Beat (via WolfStreet / Fed G.19)
items.title: Average auto loan hit a record $42,500 — up 70% from a decade of stability at $25K
items.idea: The average amount financed by auto loans held steady around $25,000 from 2008-2014, then grew dramatically to a new record of $42,500 in Q1 2026. Separately, June consumer credit jumped $14.17BN (fully reversing May's $1.1BN drop, the first decline since late 2024), driven by a rebound in revolving credit — even as the average credit card interest rate rose to 22.15%, a level last seen three years ago when Fed funds was ~2 points higher.
items.angle: Consumers are paying near-record rates on record-sized loans and still increasing revolving debt — that combination is the setup for credit-cycle stress if labor income growth (already slowing per the NFP data) doesn't keep pace.
items.tweetA: Auto loan size is up 70% in a decade to a record $42,500. Credit card rates are at 22.15%, last seen when Fed funds was 2 points higher. Consumers are borrowing more at a worse rate than the last time rates were this high — that gap is the thing to watch, not the headline NFP number.
items.tweetB: Consumer credit fully reversed May's decline in a single month, driven by revolving debt, the same week wage growth slowed to 3.2% y/y. Spending is outrunning income growth again — usually a late-cycle tell, not an early-cycle one.

items.title: 8.58 million Americans work two jobs — and it's actually near a 10-year low
items.idea: WolfStreet's July multiple-jobholder breakdown: 8.58M people (5.3% of total employment), the lowest since late 2024 and squarely mid-range of the 40-year historical range. Of them, 55% combine full-time and part-time work, 25% hold two part-time jobs with no full-time job, and only 5.5% hold two full-time jobs.
items.angle: This directly undercuts a common 'gig economy exploding, everyone needs two jobs to survive' narrative that recirculates every time jobs data disappoints — the actual multiple-jobholder rate is unremarkable by historical standards.
items.tweetA: Every time jobs data disappoints, 'everyone needs two jobs now' narratives resurface. The actual multiple-jobholder rate right now: 5.3%, near a 10-year low, dead center of the 40-year range. The vibes and the data are pointing in opposite directions this week.
items.tweetB: Only 5.5% of multiple jobholders have two full-time jobs. The other 94.5% are a full-time+part-time or two-part-time combo — a very different economic story (flexibility, side income) than the 'overworked and underpaid' framing usually attached to this stat.
